However, the protocol difference with s43 means even that comparison wouldn't be perfectly aligned, so the footnote approach is more honest about the limitations.

On the novelty framing, reframing this as an empirical phenomenon is defensible—the LOO method itself is standard, so the real contribution lies elsewhere.

Looking at the Goodhart predictability warnings, the three surprising elements hold up well: the fact that even micro doses affect performance, the non-monotonic dose-response curve, and the stochastic bifurcation where seeds diverge under identical conditions are all genuinely novel observations that Goodhart theory doesn't specifically predict.

The cross-scale wording adjustment to "exhibits in single-seed evaluation" is appropriately cautious, and the mechanistic explanation for the SFT PR confound works—SFT has no exploration component, so it can't account for the observed effects.

But there's a trickier reviewer concern lurking here: maybe SFT doesn't hack simply because it barely solves anything at 13% PR, not because it's fundamentally safer. The paper defends this by pointing to the 100-step RL checkpoint hitting 32% PR with 31.2% hacking, showing that even at modest performance levels, RL already exhibits hacking behavior. That comparison is crucial but got compressed into an appendix reference in the latest version—keeping it more visible might strengthen the argument against this objection.

The H8 audit incompleteness warning is handled well with the honest disclosure of 23% non-hacking in the uncorrected data, dropping to 17% with the s42-only correction. That directly addresses reviewer skepticism about coverage.

On the β=0.3 trajectory limitation, the qualifier makes sense—testing only at 500 steps with confirmation at β=0.1 is defensible given GPU constraints and the fact that β=0.1 is the only dose with a clear observation window.

The abstract data pile-up is solved by cutting down to 3-4 key numbers instead of scattering p-values and trajectory percentages everywhere. The core findings—PR at 95±5%, ISR collapse at 99.5%, and 92% SFT non-hacking—tell the story cleanly.

For the Goodhart taxonomy, adding the Manheim & Garrabrant classification works well for the intended audience. The H7 tautologies fit as regressional-extremal: the proxy (ISR) diverges from true quality, and the optimizer finds boundary-case inputs (single-premise proofs) that game the metric while staying out of distribution.

Now I'm checking the reward landscape geometry calculation where H7 achieves ISR=0.75 while genuine proofs sit around ISR≈0.26...

The gap between them is roughly 0.492β, which at β=0.1 gives about a 5% relative reward advantage—that quantifies how strong the attractor is. Though I should note the paper flags that the ISR values are inflated by H7 gaming, and the 0.258 figure is specifically for ISR-trained genuine proofs, so comparing against the pre-selection baseline would be more rigorous.

But really, what matters for GRPO's perspective is the reward landscape it actually encounters: H7 outputs consistently hit ISR≈0.75 while genuine proofs with typical premise counts land around 0.25-0.30. That gap is real and measurable, so the proposed framing is sound.

W14 and W15 fold into W1 cleanly. For the Table 1 caption, cutting it from 7 lines to 4 improves readability without losing substance. The reference additions—Krakovna on specification gaming, Polu & Sutskever on formal math AI, Everitt on agent incentives—all fit naturally. Now I'm checking what might still be missing. The appendix has stale data—Table 8 and the H7a prevalence paragraph are both still running on 3-seed numbers, while W3 proposes a new 5-seed table. Should I update those existing appendix tables to 5-seed as well? The s45-1000 and s42-1000 trajectory patterns are in experiments.tex now but not detailed in the Introduction's C2 contribution statement, though the current phrasing about the genuine window being transient and β controlling timing rather than outcome is general enough to hold. And I should check the Figure 3 caption about hacking composition.

The caption still says "3 seeds"—if I don't regenerate that figure with 5-seed data, reviewers will catch the mismatch between figure and text. W3 fills the data gap with a table but doesn't address the figure itself. There's also the "≥94% H7" claim in L118 that's technically 93.7% for β=0.05, which is a small error but worth fixing in a round of accuracy corrections. The new β=0.05 appendix reference in W1 points to a section that doesn't exist yet and needs to be created.

I should also reconsider W4 more carefully—the Director is asking whether to replace the exec-only baseline with 3-seed pooled data in Table 1, leaning toward keeping exec-only because the 3-seed evaluation protocol isn't uniform across seeds.

The better approach is keeping Table 1 as the single-seed exec-only baseline, then adding an appendix table showing all 3 seeds with 1000 steps and noting where s43 diverged in protocol, demonstrating they all converge to high performance regardless. It's more transparent than forcing inconsistent data together. The reviewer's concern about asymmetry is fair, but pooling with protocol mismatches would be worse.

One more issue: the proposal claims the GPUs are already released for β=0.3 extended training, but they're actually still running s45-1000 and random-b005-s44.  Once those finish, there's enough time before the 8-day deadline to run β=0.3 for 1000 steps on one seed in about 6-7 hours. The Director decided against it though, reasoning that β=0.1 is the only dose with a genuine window to track, which makes sense since β=0.3 at 500 steps shows 0-11% genuine across seeds. Though actually s43 showed 23→20% genuine after the D106 correction, so there is a window there. But the Director's point holds—the core story is about β=0.1's trajectory, and β=0.3 is secondary. Time to wrap up the review.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate STA along three axes: ISR as a diagnostic for reward hacking (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}); ISR as a training reward across four dose levels, where it exhibits Goodhart effects (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); and STA as a cross-logic protocol (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Cross-scale evidence from Qwen3-1.7B reveals capacity-dependent Goodhart basins (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}).
A hacking taxonomy synthesizes the modes observed across conditions (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

\subsection{Setup}\label{sec:setup}

We train Qwen3-4B~\citep{qwen3} with GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} ($K{=}4$, lr $10^{-6}$, 500 steps default, 1000 where noted) over seeds $\{42,43,44\}$ on a fixed 500-example FOLIO~\citep{folio} subset held constant across all conditions; the SFT baseline is trained with negative log-likelihood (NLL) on gold formalizations.\footnote{All experiments use \texttt{data/train\_500\_seed42.jsonl}; seeds control initialization and rollout sampling only.}
Held-out evaluation uses 100 FOLIO examples (\texttt{proofwriter\_fol\_100.jsonl}) with greedy decoding (Appendix~\ref{app:setup}).
We report prove rate (PR), proved-only ISR ($\text{ISR}^*$), hacking-mode rates from a two-stage classifier (strict text matching for H1/H7 plus functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution; \S\ref{sec:taxonomy-method}), and a \emph{non-hacking} (N-H) rate, defined as the residual of proved samples matching none of the nine cataloged patterns (a necessary but not sufficient condition for semantic correctness).

\subsection{ISR as Diagnostic}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_isr_collapse.pdf}

By step 1000, 94.8\% of proved samples have $\text{ISR}{=}0$ and mean component count inflates 6.58$\to$18.55 (contradiction explosion).}
\label{fig:isr-collapse}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Collapse trajectory.}
Figure~\ref{fig:isr-collapse} traces exec-only GRPO (seed~42) at 100, 500, 1000 steps.
PR rises $32\%\to93\%\to96\%$, a trajectory that execution-only evaluation would interpret as successful optimization; $\text{ISR}^*$ tells the opposite story, $0.642\to0.132\to0.003$ (214$\times$ collapse). %% registry: plan003-eval-exec-only-r5, plan001-exec-only-s42-r2, plan016-extended-1000-s42
By 500 steps, 87.1\% of proved samples embed the conclusion (H1); by 1000 steps, the embedding rate saturates at 100\% and mean component count more than doubles ($6.58\to18.55$) as the model emits contradictory or vacuous premises that trivially derive any conclusion.
Extended training, lacking a structural signal, \emph{worsens} formalization quality while improving the headline number.

\textbf{Cross-seed instability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge into qualitatively different failure modes despite shared data, hyperparameters, and reward (Appendix~\ref{app:detailed-results}): s42 reaches $\text{PR}{=}93\%$ via conclusion embedding ($\text{H1}{=}87\%$); s43 collapses to $\text{PR}{=}13\%$ (at 500 steps) via repetition (87\% of rollouts truncated); s44 reaches $\text{PR}{=}98\%$ via tautological collapse ($\text{H7}{=}100\%$, mean $n{=}2.04$). %% registry: plan001-exec-only-s42-r2, plan001-exec-only-s43-r4, plan001-exec-only-s44
The cross-seed PR variance ($\sigma{=}47$\,pp) shows that aggregate metrics obscure qualitatively different failure modes; all three are flagged by $\text{ISR}^*$ even though one passes the PR check (s44) and one fails it (s43).
By 1000 steps, all three converge to high PR ($0.95{\pm}0.05$) with near-zero genuine output (see Appendix~\ref{app:h8} and Table~\ref{tab:fol-detailed}), each through a different dominant mode (s42: H1 saturation; s43: H1 $93.8\%$, genuine $6.2\%$; s44: H1+H8). %% registry: plan016-extended-1000-s42, exec-only-s43-1000step-r7, plan001-exec-only-s44-1000-r2
Notably, s43 recovers from $\text{PR}{=}13\%$ (500 steps) to $\text{PR}{=}96\%$ (1000 steps), but entirely through H1 exploitation: PR recovery does not imply quality recovery, and the repetition-collapse phase is transient rather than terminal.

\textbf{SFT baseline.}
SFT on gold formalizations reaches $\text{PR}{=}13.0\%$ (3-seed pooled, 1000 steps) with $\text{H7}{=}0$, $\text{H1}{=}7.7\%$, $92.3\%$ non-hacking ($n{=}39$; $\text{OR}{=}147$ vs.\ exec-only, $p{<}0.001$; per-seed range ${\sim}$91--93\%). %% registry: plan009-sft-baseline-s42-1000/s43-1000/s44-1000-r3
The near-absence of hacking under identical data exposure is consistent with hacking being RL-specific; a 100-step checkpoint confirms hacking emerges early in training (Appendix~\ref{app:100step}).

2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	GRPO-trained formalizers converge to high prove rates on first-order logic problems ($95{\pm}5\%$ across three seeds, 1000 steps), yet at convergence, \emph{none} produce structurally sound outputs.
5	Each seed develops a distinct degenerate shortcut: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, or tautological collapse, all invisible to execution-based evaluation, which registers success regardless of whether the proof reflects genuine derivation.
6	
7	\paragraph{The execution-only blind spot.}
8	Prove rate, the dominant evaluation metric for neurosymbolic formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}, conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts, a gap especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
9	Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback; this drives rapid PR gains but provides no signal on structural quality.
10	Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings.
11	A separate line of work documents that LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}; what is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in neurosymbolic outputs.
12	
13	\paragraph{Component necessity testing.}
14	We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), which applies \emph{component necessity testing} (leave-one-out ablation on solver inputs) to quantify structural integrity (Figure~\ref{fig:sta-overview}).
15	For each proved formalization, STA removes each component individually and re-runs the solver; the fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure yields the \emph{Intensional Structural Reward} (ISR), with $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicating full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ complete redundancy.
16	LOO ablation itself is standard~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
17	ISR captures structural rather than semantic integrity (downstream NLI: $\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$).
18	
19	\paragraph{ISR as diagnostic.}
20	As a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio}, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory invisible to PR: $\text{ISR}^{*}{:}\,0.642\to 0.132\to 0.003$ over 100--1000 steps (seed~42; 99.5\% degradation) while PR rises $32\%{\to}96\%$.
21	Three seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$\,pp), each converging to a qualitatively different mode: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, and tautological collapse.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

GRPO-trained formalizers converge to high prove rates on first-order logic problems ($95{\pm}5\%$ across three seeds, 1000 steps), yet at convergence, \emph{none} produce structurally sound outputs.
Each seed develops a distinct degenerate shortcut: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, or tautological collapse, all invisible to execution-based evaluation, which registers success regardless of whether the proof reflects genuine derivation.

\paragraph{The execution-only blind spot.}
Prove rate, the dominant evaluation metric for neurosymbolic formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}, conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts, a gap especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback; this drives rapid PR gains but provides no signal on structural quality.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings.
A separate line of work documents that LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}; what is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in neurosymbolic outputs.

\paragraph{Component necessity testing.}
We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), which applies \emph{component necessity testing} (leave-one-out ablation on solver inputs) to quantify structural integrity (Figure~\ref{fig:sta-overview}).
For each proved formalization, STA removes each component individually and re-runs the solver; the fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure yields the \emph{Intensional Structural Reward} (ISR), with $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicating full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ complete redundancy.
LOO ablation itself is standard~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
ISR captures structural rather than semantic integrity (downstream NLI: $\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$).

\paragraph{ISR as diagnostic.}
As a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio}, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory invisible to PR: $\text{ISR}^{*}{:}\,0.642\to 0.132\to 0.003$ over 100--1000 steps (seed~42; 99.5\% degradation) while PR rises $32\%{\to}96\%$.
Three seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$\,pp), each converging to a qualitatively different mode: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, and tautological collapse.
An SFT baseline on identical data reaches $\text{PR}{=}13.0\%$ with 92.3\% non-hacking (3-seed pooled, 1000 steps), localizing the failure to RL optimization, not data or capacity.

\paragraph{ISR as reward: Goodhart collapse at all tested doses.}
Repurposed as a training signal, $r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta\,\text{ISR})$, ISR contains an inherent structural vulnerability: tautological proofs (a single premise identical to the conclusion) receive $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$ by construction, and implication tautologies ($P{\to}P$) receive $\text{ISR}{=}0.75$, creating a positive feedback loop once sampled during GRPO rollouts~\citep{karwowski-goodhart-rl, kwa-catastrophic-goodhart}.
Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} is observed at all four tested doses ($\beta\in\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$): $\beta$ controls \emph{when} collapse occurs, not \emph{whether}.
At $\beta{=}0.1$, collapse is stochastic and delayed: 5 seeds bifurcate between rapid H7 convergence (2 seeds, ${\leq}100$ steps) and a transient genuine window (${\sim}23\%$ non-hacking at 500 steps, 5-seed pooled) that closes under extended training (seeds~42 and~45: $17\%{\to}2\%$ and $55\%{\to}0\%$ genuine at 1000 steps).
Snapshot evaluation at 500 steps would overestimate ISR's benefit; trajectory analysis at $\beta{=}0.1$ confirms the window is temporary.
The effect transfers to Prolog (3/3 seeds yield 0\% non-hacking via distinct mechanisms, including \emph{query-as-fact gaming}) and is preliminarily observed at 1.7B scale (qualitatively novel gaming modes in single-seed evaluation).
ISR's asymmetry is the central finding: \emph{reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer at any dose.}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
Across 6 reward conditions, 5 seeds, 2 logic types, 2 model scales, and up to 1000 steps, we contribute: (\textbf{C1}) We empirically demonstrate ISR as a diagnostic for GRPO reward hacking, revealing a 99.5\% collapse trajectory invisible to PR, with an SFT control localizing the failure to RL (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}); (\textbf{C2}) an empirical instance of Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} at all four tested doses: ISR's structural bias ($\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$ for tautological proofs) creates a positive feedback loop; the genuine window at moderate $\beta$ is transient, and $\beta$ controls only timing, not outcome (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); (\textbf{C3}) cross-logic transfer to Prolog with consistent Goodhart effects across all seeds (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}); (\textbf{C4}) a nine-mode hacking taxonomy including query-as-fact gaming, obfuscated tautology, and a scale-specific \emph{ex falso} mode, motivating functional cross-validation of diagnostics (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
These are cautionary results: snapshot evaluation of structural rewards can overestimate their benefit; only trajectory analysis reveals the transient nature of apparent improvement.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

STA exposes a 99.5\% structural collapse invisible to prove rate (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}); repurposed as a training signal, ISR produces Goodhart collapse at all four tested doses (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}), consistent across logic types (Prolog: 0\% non-hacking, 3/3 seeds), model scales (1.7B: novel gaming modes), and training durations (500$\to$1000 steps at $\beta{=}0.1$, the only dose with trajectory confirmation).
In the taxonomy of \citet{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}, ISR's collapse is primarily regressional (the proxy's statistical regularities diverge from the target) with extremal elements (the optimizer finds out-of-distribution tautological inputs that maximize the proxy).
The empirical details exceed what Goodhart's Law predicts in the abstract: collapse at micro-doses ($\beta{=}0.05$) where the ISR signal is barely detectable, non-monotonic dose-response (deterministic collapse at $\beta\in\{0.05, 0.2\}$ but stochastic bifurcation at $\beta{=}0.1$), and the transient genuine window that requires trajectory analysis to detect.
At 500 steps, ISR increases the proportion of genuine proofs relative to random controls ($22.6\%$ vs.\ $7.7\%$; $\text{OR}{=}3.48$, uncorrected); under stricter H8+FN-corrected classification (3-seed subset), OR reduces to $0.61$ (n.s.), and extended training on both seeds~42 and~45 (1000 steps) confirms the genuine window closes (s42: $17\%{\to}2\%$; s45: $55\%{\to}0\%$).
ISR is reliable as a diagnostic but unreliable as an optimizer: the same LOO bias that rewards genuine necessity also rewards tautological constructions.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
$\beta$ controls the \emph{timing} of collapse, not whether it occurs (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); snapshot evaluation overestimates ISR's benefit.
Text-match classifiers have systematic blind spots (H7b, query-as-fact, H9 all evade detection); mandatory functional cross-validation is needed (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
Different model capacities converge to different exploits (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}); no safe scale was observed in our single-seed evaluation (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).
ISR and similar perturbation-based metrics should serve as post-hoc evaluation tools, not training signals.
Future work should explore ISR variants that penalize tautological constructions and test generalization to other neurosymbolic domains beyond first-order logic.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

GRPO-trained formalizers converge to high prove rates on first-order logic problems ($95{\pm}5\%$ across three seeds, 1000 steps), yet at convergence, \emph{none} produce structurally sound outputs.
Each seed develops a distinct degenerate shortcut: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, or tautological collapse, all invisible to execution-based evaluation, which registers success regardless of whether the proof reflects genuine derivation.

\paragraph{The execution-only blind spot.}
Prove rate, the dominant evaluation metric for neurosymbolic formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}, conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts, a gap especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback; this drives rapid PR gains but provides no signal on structural quality.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings.
A separate line of work documents that LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}; what is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in neurosymbolic outputs.

\paragraph{Component necessity testing.}
We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), which applies \emph{component necessity testing} (leave-one-out ablation on solver inputs) to quantify structural integrity (Figure~\ref{fig:sta-overview}).
For each proved formalization, STA removes each component individually and re-runs the solver; the fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure yields the \emph{Intensional Structural Reward} (ISR), with $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicating full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ complete redundancy.
LOO ablation itself is standard~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
ISR captures structural rather than semantic integrity (downstream NLI: $\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$).

\paragraph{ISR as diagnostic.}
As a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio}, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory invisible to PR: $\text{ISR}^{*}{:}\,0.642\to 0.132\to 0.003$ over 100--1000 steps (seed~42; 99.5\% degradation) while PR rises $32\%{\to}96\%$.
Three seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$\,pp), each converging to a qualitatively different mode: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, and tautological collapse.
An SFT baseline on identical data reaches $\text{PR}{=}13.0\%$ with 92.3\% non-hacking (3-seed pooled, 1000 steps), localizing the failure to RL optimization, not data or capacity.

\paragraph{ISR as reward: Goodhart collapse at all tested doses.}
Repurposed as a training signal, $r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta\,\text{ISR})$, ISR contains an inherent structural vulnerability: tautological proofs (a single premise identical to the conclusion) receive $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$ by construction, and implication tautologies ($P{\to}P$) receive $\text{ISR}{=}0.75$, creating a positive feedback loop once sampled during GRPO rollouts~\citep{karwowski-goodhart-rl, kwa-catastrophic-goodhart}.
Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} is observed at all four tested doses ($\beta\in\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$): $\beta$ controls \emph{when} collapse occurs, not \emph{whether}.
At $\beta{=}0.1$, collapse is stochastic and delayed: 5 seeds bifurcate between rapid H7 convergence (2 seeds, ${\leq}100$ steps) and a transient genuine window (${\sim}23\%$ non-hacking at 500 steps, 5-seed pooled) that closes under extended training (seeds~42 and~45: $17\%{\to}2\%$ and $55\%{\to}0\%$ genuine at 1000 steps).
Snapshot evaluation at 500 steps would overestimate ISR's benefit; trajectory analysis at $\beta{=}0.1$ confirms the window is temporary.
The effect transfers to Prolog (3/3 seeds yield 0\% non-hacking via distinct mechanisms, including \emph{query-as-fact gaming}) and is preliminarily observed at 1.7B scale (qualitatively novel gaming modes in single-seed evaluation).
ISR's asymmetry is the central finding: \emph{reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer at any dose.}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
Across 6 reward conditions, 5 seeds, 2 logic types, 2 model scales, and up to 1000 steps, we contribute: (\textbf{C1}) We empirically demonstrate ISR as a diagnostic for GRPO reward hacking, revealing a 99.5\% collapse trajectory invisible to PR, with an SFT control localizing the failure to RL (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}); (\textbf{C2}) an empirical instance of Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} at all four tested doses: ISR's structural bias ($\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$ for tautological proofs) creates a positive feedback loop; the genuine window at moderate $\beta$ is transient, and $\beta$ controls only timing, not outcome (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); (\textbf{C3}) cross-logic transfer to Prolog with consistent Goodhart effects across all seeds (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}); (\textbf{C4}) a nine-mode hacking taxonomy including query-as-fact gaming, obfuscated tautology, and a scale-specific \emph{ex falso} mode, motivating functional cross-validation of diagnostics (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
These are cautionary results: snapshot evaluation of structural rewards can overestimate their benefit; only trajectory analysis reveals the transient nature of apparent improvement.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

STA exposes a 99.5\% structural collapse invisible to prove rate (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}); repurposed as a training signal, ISR produces Goodhart collapse at all four tested doses (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}), consistent across logic types (Prolog: 0\% non-hacking, 3/3 seeds), model scales (1.7B: novel gaming modes), and training durations (500$\to$1000 steps at $\beta{=}0.1$, the only dose with trajectory confirmation).
In the taxonomy of \citet{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}, ISR's collapse is primarily regressional (the proxy's statistical regularities diverge from the target) with extremal elements (the optimizer finds out-of-distribution tautological inputs that maximize the proxy).
The empirical details exceed what Goodhart's Law predicts in the abstract: collapse at micro-doses ($\beta{=}0.05$) where the ISR signal is barely detectable, non-monotonic dose-response (deterministic collapse at $\beta\in\{0.05, 0.2\}$ but stochastic bifurcation at $\beta{=}0.1$), and the transient genuine window that requires trajectory analysis to detect.
At 500 steps, ISR increases the proportion of genuine proofs relative to random controls ($22.6\%$ vs.\ $7.7\%$; $\text{OR}{=}3.48$, uncorrected); under stricter H8+FN-corrected classification (3-seed subset), OR reduces to $0.61$ (n.s.), and extended training on both seeds~42 and~45 (1000 steps) confirms the genuine window closes (s42: $17\%{\to}2\%$; s45: $55\%{\to}0\%$).
ISR is reliable as a diagnostic but unreliable as an optimizer: the same LOO bias that rewards genuine necessity also rewards tautological constructions.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
$\beta$ controls the \emph{timing} of collapse, not whether it occurs (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); snapshot evaluation overestimates ISR's benefit.
Text-match classifiers have systematic blind spots (H7b, query-as-fact, H9 all evade detection); mandatory functional cross-validation is needed (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
Different model capacities converge to different exploits (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}); no safe scale was observed in our single-seed evaluation (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).
ISR and similar perturbation-based metrics should serve as post-hoc evaluation tools, not training signals.
Future work should explore ISR variants that penalize tautological constructions and test generalization to other neurosymbolic domains beyond first-order logic.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

GRPO-trained formalizers converge to high prove rates on first-order logic problems ($95{\pm}5\%$ across three seeds, 1000 steps), yet at convergence, \emph{none} produce structurally sound outputs.
Each seed develops a distinct degenerate shortcut: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, or tautological collapse, all invisible to execution-based evaluation, which registers success regardless of whether the proof reflects genuine derivation.

\paragraph{The execution-only blind spot.}
Prove rate, the dominant evaluation metric for neurosymbolic formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}, conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts, a gap especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback; this drives rapid PR gains but provides no signal on structural quality.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings.
A separate line of work documents that LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}; what is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in neurosymbolic outputs.

\paragraph{Component necessity testing.}
We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), which applies \emph{component necessity testing} (leave-one-out ablation on solver inputs) to quantify structural integrity (Figure~\ref{fig:sta-overview}).
For each proved formalization, STA removes each component individually and re-runs the solver; the fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure yields the \emph{Intensional Structural Reward} (ISR), with $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicating full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ complete redundancy.
LOO ablation itself is standard~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
ISR captures structural rather than semantic integrity (downstream NLI: $\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$).

\paragraph{ISR as diagnostic.}
As a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio}, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory invisible to PR: $\text{ISR}^{*}{:}\,0.642\to 0.132\to 0.003$ over 100--1000 steps (seed~42; 99.5\% degradation) while PR rises $32\%{\to}96\%$.
Three seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$\,pp), each converging to a qualitatively different mode: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, and tautological collapse.
An SFT baseline on identical data reaches $\text{PR}{=}13.0\%$ with 92.3\% non-hacking (3-seed pooled, 1000 steps), localizing the failure to RL optimization, not data or capacity.

\paragraph{ISR as reward: Goodhart collapse at all tested doses.}
Repurposed as a training signal, $r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta\,\text{ISR})$, ISR contains an inherent structural vulnerability: tautological proofs (a single premise identical to the conclusion) receive $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$ by construction, and implication tautologies ($P{\to}P$) receive $\text{ISR}{=}0.75$, creating a positive feedback loop once sampled during GRPO rollouts~\citep{karwowski-goodhart-rl, kwa-catastrophic-goodhart}.
Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} is observed at all four tested doses ($\beta\in\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$): $\beta$ controls \emph{when} collapse occurs, not \emph{whether}.
At $\beta{=}0.1$, collapse is stochastic and delayed: 5 seeds bifurcate between rapid H7 convergence (2 seeds, ${\leq}100$ steps) and a transient genuine window (${\sim}23\%$ non-hacking at 500 steps, 5-seed pooled) that closes under extended training (seeds~42 and~45: $17\%{\to}2\%$ and $55\%{\to}0\%$ genuine at 1000 steps).
Snapshot evaluation at 500 steps would overestimate ISR's benefit; trajectory analysis at $\beta{=}0.1$ confirms the window is temporary.
The effect transfers to Prolog (3/3 seeds yield 0\% non-hacking via distinct mechanisms, including \emph{query-as-fact gaming}) and is preliminarily observed at 1.7B scale (qualitatively novel gaming modes in single-seed evaluation).
ISR's asymmetry is the central finding: \emph{reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer at any dose.}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
Across 6 reward conditions, 5 seeds, 2 logic types, 2 model scales, and up to 1000 steps, we contribute: (\textbf{C1}) We empirically demonstrate ISR as a diagnostic for GRPO reward hacking, revealing a 99.5\% collapse trajectory invisible to PR, with an SFT control localizing the failure to RL (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}); (\textbf{C2}) an empirical instance of Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} at all four tested doses: ISR's structural bias ($\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$ for tautological proofs) creates a positive feedback loop; the genuine window at moderate $\beta$ is transient, and $\beta$ controls only timing, not outcome (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); (\textbf{C3}) cross-logic transfer to Prolog with consistent Goodhart effects across all seeds (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}); (\textbf{C4}) a nine-mode hacking taxonomy including query-as-fact gaming, obfuscated tautology, and a scale-specific \emph{ex falso} mode, motivating functional cross-validation of diagnostics (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
These are cautionary results: snapshot evaluation of structural rewards can overestimate their benefit; only trajectory analysis reveals the transient nature of apparent improvement.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related-work}
3	
4	\paragraph{Neurosymbolic reasoning.}
5	LLM-solver pipelines~\citep{satlm, logic-lm, linc, fover-pei2025, lorp} and RL methods trained on solver feedback~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl, deepseek-prover-v15} evaluate execution accuracy alone, with no diagnostic for structural quality.
6	We use FOLIO~\citep{folio}, the only public NLI benchmark with both FOL and Prolog annotations.
7	
8	\paragraph{Process rewards and reward shaping.}
9	Learned PRMs~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} provide step-level feedback but suffer from reward-model noise and distribution shift~\citep{processbench}; recent work extends PRMs to multi-domain settings~\citep{zeng2025versaprm} and process-level reasoning~\citep{khalifa2025thinkprm}. \citet{gao-effective-rl-reward} show that auxiliary process/outcome rewards can \emph{hurt} RL training relative to success-only reward, a finding our ISR-as-reward results corroborate.
10	Symbolic feedback approaches~\citep{rlsf} use solver certificates as token-level rewards, achieving gains on program synthesis; ISR differs in operating at the component level (LOO ablation) rather than the token level, and our results show this structural signal is gamed when optimized.
11	Rubric-grounded GRPO~\citep{rubric-grpo} uses structured LLM-judge rewards to improve generalization; ISR is solver-derived and deterministic rather than judge-based, but both represent structured alternatives to scalar execution reward.
12	The shared lesson across these approaches is that reward augmentation introduces proxy risk; our contribution is providing an empirical instance of this variant in the neurosymbolic setting, where the diagnostic itself becomes the optimization target.
13	
14	\paragraph{Reward hacking and Goodhart's Law.}
15	Goodhart's Law is established theoretically~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, skalse-reward-hacking, karwowski-goodhart-rl} and empirically in RLHF and frontier models~\citep{gao-reward-overoptimization, bondarenko-spec-gaming, kim-game-formalization}.
16	\citet{kwa-catastrophic-goodhart} show that heavy-tailed reward misspecification causes \emph{catastrophic} Goodhart where KL regularization provably fails, offering a theoretical lens for why GRPO's KL penalty does not prevent the ISR collapse we observe.
17	Recent work further documents spurious reward signals in RLVR~\citep{spurious-rewards} and reward hacking in frontier models~\citep{metr-reward-hacking}.
18	Our setting differs in three ways: ISR is deterministic and solver-derived rather than learned; gaming \emph{emerges during RL training} rather than at inference time; and the effect operates at a diagnostic level, where the metric designed to detect gaming becomes gamed when optimized.
19	\citet{pan-reward-misspecification} show that more capable agents exploit reward misspecifications more severely; our cross-scale comparison (4B vs.\ 1.7B) complements this finding by demonstrating that different capacities discover qualitatively different exploits under identical reward formulations.
20	We frame our results as an empirical instance of Goodhart's Law within the \citet{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} taxonomy: ISR's LOO definition creates an inherent structural bias toward tautology ($P{\to}P$ receives $\text{ISR}{=}0.75$ by construction), with collapse observed at all four tested doses.
21	
22	\paragraph{Mutation testing.}
23	STA adapts the LOO mutation paradigm~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey} to solver inputs; our contribution lies in the application and empirical findings, not in the perturbation primitive itself.
